Opel's New Astra Start Base Trim Comes With Hub-Capped Steelies Despite Retailing From €31,890
14 photos
Photo: Opel
Opel just made its cheapest Astra a great deal cheaper, and the new Start grade barely gives anything up to shave €1,500 off its predecessor. €1,900 more affordable than before in full-electric flavor, the Start's only real downgrade is the switch to 16-inch steel wheels and some plasticky covers for good measure.
The internal combustion Astra Start and its electric sibling currently start at €31,890 and €36,490 in Germany, including the value-added tax. Patrick Dinger, the head of the brand in Germany, claims the Start is extensively equipped while playing a superior affordability card than many direct competitors. But looking at the bigger picture, over 30,000 euros for a compact still is a lot of money.
Beyond the footwear giveaway, the Start is very similar to the Edition grade. An illuminated Vizor grille is standard, as are LED taillights, LED front lighting units, Intelli-Seats with six-way adjustments and central cushion recesses, LED interior lighting, automatic climate control, and keyless start. Of course, Opel saved a few euros by offering a four-speaker DAB+ radio instead of a higher-quality setup.
Speaking of quality, there are no conventional gauges to speak of. Customers get a pair of 10-inch displays, one handling the instrumentation and the other all things infotainment. Considering that Opel's lesser Frontera Start comes with a smartphone mount instead of an infotainment screen, the Astra Start is the better pick. Front and rear parking sensors also need mentioning, and Opel further made a case for a new paint color.
Denim Blue is a metallic shade that enters the palette at no additional cost. While it may feature basic ADAS, the rearview camera is nowhere to be seen. Thankfully, the rear-facing sensors will come in handy in tight spaces. Another curiosity of the Astra Start is transmission choices. Instead of an honest manual, all powertrains get two-pedal setups.
Photo: Opel The most affordable of Astra Start models is a mild-hybrid turbo 1.2-liter i3 with 143 horsepower to its name. In optimal conditions, this powertrain generates 230 Newton-meters (170 pound-feet) of twist. A six-speed electrified tranny does the shifting. Buyers who do serious highway miles can pick a turbo diesel with around 130 ponies on tap, which includes a torque converter and eight forward ratios.
Upgrading to the Astra Start electric gets you 154 mechanical horsepower and no more than 270 Newton-meters (almost 200 pound-feet) of near-instant torque. Vehicle-to-load capability is listed, though it needs an official adapter. The Start cannot be had as a plug-in hybrid, and that may be a missed opportunity when you remember how versatile PHEVs are.
Available in hatchback and wagon formats, the German model sips 4.7 to 5.1 liters of gasoline per 100 clicks on the WLTP. That's 46 to 50 miles per gallon US. The full-electric alternative packs a 55.4-kWh battery that offers a WLTP-estimated 454 kilometers (282 miles) of range.
Customers who can't do without alloys have to spend an extra €800 for 16s mounted with all-season rubber. The Comfort Pack is the more interesting option, though, for it bundles heat-shielding windows, a center armrest, an auto-dimming function for the central rearview mirror, and wagon-only roof rails.
